Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 57, verse 1–3:

Surah al-Hadid is Madinan according to all scholars, and it has twenty-nine verses. From al-Irbad ibn Sariyah: the Prophet (ﷺ) used to recite the musabbihat (the surahs beginning with glorification of God) before sleeping, and he would say: "Indeed, among them there is a verse better than a thousand verses." He meant by the musabbihat: al-Hadid, al-Hashr, al-Saff, al-Jumu'ah, and al-Taghabun.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies God, and He is the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ (1) ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He gives life and causes death, and He is over all things Powerful.﴾ (2) ﴿He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden, and He is, of all things, Knowing.﴾ (3)

God's saying: ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies God﴾, meaning: it glorifies God and declares Him free of imperfection. Ibn Abbas said: "prays to God" (sallā lillāh). (Whatever is in the heavens) from among the angels who were created, (and the earth) from whatever has a soul or does not have a soul in it. It was also said: this is the glorification of indication (tasbih al-dalalah). Al-Zajjaj rejected this and said: if this were the glorification of indication and the manifestation of the traces of creation, it would be understood; so why did He say: ﴿but you do not understand their glorification﴾ [see vol. 10, p. 266]? Rather, it is glorification of speech. He cited God's saying: ﴿And We subjected the mountains to glorify [God] with David﴾ [see vol. 11, p. 307]. If this were glorification of indication, what would be the specificity for David?! I say: what he mentioned is the correct view, and its explanation and discussion have passed under (Subhan) [see vol. 10, p. 266 onward], at God's saying: ﴿And there is not a thing but that it glorifies Him with His praise﴾. (The Mighty, the Wise.) God's saying: meaning He alone possesses that. Dominion (al-mulk) is an expression for sovereignty and the executing of command; He, glorified is He, is the King, the Capable, the Dominant. It was also said: it refers to the treasuries of rain, plants and all sustenance.

(He gives life and causes death) He causes the living to die in this world and gives life to the dead for resurrection. It was also said: He gives life to drops of semen, which are dead, and causes the living to die. The position of (He gives life and causes death) is in the nominative, meaning "and He gives life and causes death." It is also permissible that it be in the accusative, meaning "to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth" as giving life and causing death, as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (lahu), with the preposition governing it.

(And He is over all things Powerful) meaning God cannot be incapacitated by anything.

God's saying: ﴿He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden﴾. Scholars differed about the meanings of these names, and we have explained them in the book al-Asna. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) explained them with an explanation that suffices against every speaker's words. He said in Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Abu Hurairah: "O God, You are the First, so nothing is before You; You are the Last, so nothing is after You; You are the Manifest, so nothing is above You; You are the Hidden, so nothing is beneath You. Settle our debt for us and enrich us from poverty." He meant by the Manifest the Dominant, and by the Hidden the Knowing, and God knows best.

(And He is, of all things, Knowing) of what has been or will be, so nothing is hidden from Him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 57, verses 4–6:

The Almighty's saying: ﴿He it is who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne﴾ has already been discussed in full in (al-A'raf) [[See vol. 7, p. 218.]].

The Almighty's saying: ﴿He knows what enters into the earth﴾, i.e. what enters it of rain and other things, (and what comes out of it) of plants and other things, (and what descends from the sky) of provision, rain and angels, (and what ascends into it) what rises up into it of angels and the deeds of the servants, (and He is with you) meaning by His power, His authority and His knowledge, (wherever you may be, and Allah is Seeing of what you do) He sees your deeds and observes them, and nothing of them is hidden from Him. In this verse He has combined (established upon the Throne) with (and He is with you). Taking both in their apparent meaning would be a contradiction, which shows that ta'wil (interpretation beyond the literal sense) is necessary, and refusing ta'wil amounts to admitting the contradiction. Imam Abu al-Ma'ali (al-Juwayni) said: On the night of the Isra' (Night Journey), Muhammad (ﷺ) was no nearer to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, than Yunus ibn Matta (Jonah) was when he was in the belly of the fish. This has already been mentioned.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾. This repetition is for emphasis, i.e. He is the one truly worthy of worship. (And to Allah are affairs returned) i.e. the affairs of creatures in the Hereafter. Al-Hasan, al-A'raj, Ya'qub, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Haywa, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, al-A'mash, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read (turja'u) with a fatha on the ta' and a kasra on the jim, i.e. (tarji'u). The rest read (turja'u).

The Almighty's saying: ﴿He causes the night to pass into the day and causes the day to pass into the night﴾ has already been discussed in (Al 'Imran) [[See vol. 4, p. 56.]].

(And He is Knower of what is within the breasts) i.e. the inner thoughts are not hidden from Him, and whoever has this attribute, it is not permissible for anyone other than Him to be worshipped.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 57, verse 7–9:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾, i.e., affirm that Allah is One and that Muhammad is His Messenger. (And spend) give in charity. It was said: spend in the way of Allah. It was said: the intended meaning is the obligatory zakat. It was said: the intended meaning is other than it, from the various forms of obedience and what draws near to it. (From that which He has made you successors in) is evidence that the origin of ownership belongs to Allah, glorified is He, and that the servant has in it only the disposal that pleases Allah, for which He rewards him with Paradise. So whoever spends from it in the rights of Allah, and spending from it is easy for him, just as a man finds it easy to spend from another's property when that person has permitted him to do so, he will have a great reward and a mighty recompense. Al-Hasan said: (successors in it) by your inheriting it from those who were before you. This indicates that these are not truly your wealth; you are in it only in the position of deputies and agents. So seize the opportunity in it by establishing the right before it is taken from you and passed on to those after you.

(So those who believe) and do righteous deeds (among you and spend) in the way of Allah (will have a great reward), which is Paradise.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what is [wrong] with you that you do not believe in Allah?﴾ This is an interrogative used for rebuke, meaning: what excuse do you have for not believing, when the proofs have been made clear?! (And the Messenger calls you) By this He showed that there is no ruling before the revelation of the sharia. Abu 'Amr recited: (and your covenant has been taken) in the passive form (not naming the agent). The rest recited it in the active form, meaning Allah took your covenant. Mujahid said: it is the first covenant, which was when they were in the loins of Adam, that Allah is your Lord and there is no god for you besides Him. It was said: He took your covenant by placing intellects in you and establishing for you the signs and proofs that call to following the Messenger. (If you are believers) i.e., since you are. It was said: i.e., if you are believers by the proofs and evidences. It was said: i.e., if you have ever believed in truth at any time, then now is the most fitting time for you to believe, since the proofs are established and the announcement of the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) has come, and his proofs are sound. It was said: if you are believers in Allah your Creator. And they used to acknowledge this. It was said: this is an address to a people who had believed, and the Prophet (ﷺ) took their covenant, and then they apostatized. And His saying: (if you are believers), i.e., if you acknowledge the conditions of faith.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who sends down to His servant clear verses﴾ He means the Qur'an. It was said: the miracles, i.e., belief in Muhammad (ﷺ) is binding upon you because of the miracles with him, and the Qur'an is the greatest and mightiest of them.

(That He may bring you out) i.e., by the Qur'an. It was said: by the Messenger. It was said: by the call.

(From darknesses) which is polytheism and disbelief (into light) which is faith.

(And indeed Allah is to you Kind and Merciful).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 57, verse 10:

In this verse there are five issues.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what is [wrong] with you that you do not spend in the way of Allah?﴾ That is, what prevents you from spending in the way of Allah, and in that which brings you closer to your Lord, while you are going to die and leave your wealth behind, and it is returning to Allah, exalted is He? So the meaning of the statement is a rebuke for not spending.

(And to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth) That is, both of them return to Him when those upon them perish, just as inheritance returns to the one entitled to it.

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest.﴾ Most of the exegetes hold that what is meant by "the conquest" is the conquest of Makkah. Al-Sha'bi and al-Zuhri said: it is the conquest of al-Hudaybiyah. Qatadah said: there were two fightings, one of which is superior to the other, and two expenditures, one of which is superior to the other; fighting and spending before the conquest of Makkah were superior to fighting and spending after it. There is an ellipsis in the statement, meaning: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest﴾ and those who spent and fought after the conquest, and it was omitted because the statement indicates it. Spending before the conquest was greater because people's need was greater due to the weakness of Islam, and doing so was then more difficult for the spenders, and the reward is in proportion to the hardship. And Allah knows best.

The third: Ashhab narrated from Malik, who said: those of merit and resolve should be given precedence, and Allah, exalted is He, has said: ﴿Not equal among you are those who spent and fought before the conquest.﴾ Al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, so in it there is clear evidence for the preference of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, and his precedence, because he was the first to accept Islam. And from Ibn Mas'ud: the first to openly display Islam with his sword was the Prophet (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr, and because he was the first to spend on the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ). And from Ibn 'Umar, who said: I was with the Prophet (ﷺ), and with him was Abu Bakr, wearing a cloak which he had fastened at his chest with a toothpick. Then Jibril descended and said: "O Prophet of Allah! Why do I see Abu Bakr wearing a cloak which he has fastened at his chest with a toothpick?" He said: "He spent his wealth on me before the conquest." He said: "Indeed Allah says to you: convey my greetings to Abu Bakr and say to him: are you content in this poverty of yours, or angry?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Abu Bakr, indeed Allah, mighty and majestic, sends you His greetings and says: are you content in this poverty of yours, or angry?" Abu Bakr said: "Shall I be angry with my Lord? I am truly pleased with my Lord! I am truly pleased with my Lord! I am truly pleased with my Lord!" He said: "Indeed Allah says to you: I am pleased with you, just as you are pleased with Me." Then Abu Bakr wept, and Jibril, peace be upon him, said: "By He who sent you, O Muhammad, with the truth, the bearers of the Throne have been fastening their garments with toothpicks since this companion of yours fastened his cloak with a toothpick." Hence the Companions placed him ahead of themselves and acknowledged his precedence and priority. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The Prophet (ﷺ) was first [[al-sabiq: the first. al-musalli: the second.]], Abu Bakr was second, and 'Umar was third. So whoever is brought to me preferring me over Abu Bakr, I will flog him the punishment for the slanderer, eighty lashes, and his testimony will be rejected. Those who came first bore greater hardship than those who came after them, and their insight was also more penetrating.

The fourth: Precedence and posteriority may occur in worldly rulings. As for rulings of the religion, 'Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded us to place people in their ranks. The greatest of ranks in status is prayer. The Prophet (ﷺ) said in his illness: "Command Abu Bakr to lead the people in prayer," the hadith. He also said: "Let the people be led by the one best in reciting the Book of Allah," and he said: "Let the older of you two lead you," from the hadith of Malik ibn al-Huwayrith, which has already passed. Al-Bukhari and other scholars understood from it that he meant seniority of rank, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Clientage belongs to the one who is greater [in status]," and he did not mean seniority of age. Malik and others said: indeed age has a right. Al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah took it into account, and it deserves to be taken into account, because when knowledge and age are combined in two equal persons, knowledge takes precedence. As for worldly rulings, they are arranged upon rulings of the religion, so whoever is given precedence in religion is given precedence in worldly matters. And among the reports: "He is not of us who does not honour our elder, show mercy to our young, and recognise the right of our scholar." And among the well-established hadith in isolated transmissions: "No young man honours an elderly man for his age except that Allah appoints for him, at his own age, someone who will honour him." They recited [[It is by Ibn 'Abd al-Samad al-Sarqusti, as in (Ahkam al-Quran) by Ibn al-'Arabi.]]:

O one who blames the elders for a vice... that has entered him through youth and arrogance,
Remember, when you wish to shame them, your grandfather, and remember your father, O son of a brother.
And know that youth is stripped away from you, and its burden is not stripped away.
Whoever does not honour the elders, may he never reach, on the day his age reaches [old age], the state of the elder.

The fifth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to each Allah has promised the best.﴾ That is, the ones who came first, those who were foremost and the leaders, and the ones who came later, those who followed; Allah promised them all Paradise, despite the differences in ranks. Ibn 'Amir read (wa-kullun) with the nominative (raf'), and it is likewise in the nominative in the codices of the people of Syria. The rest read (wa-kullan) with the accusative (nasb), in accordance with what is in their codices. Whoever reads it in the accusative does so because the verb falls upon it, meaning: Allah promised each the best. Whoever reads it in the nominative does so because when the object is placed first, it weakens the governing power of the verb, and the pronoun is omitted from (wa'adahu).

Allah Almighty says: ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan﴾. This urges spending in the way of Allah. The discussion of it has already passed in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 3 p. (237)]]. The Arabs say of anyone who does a good deed: "He has lent (aqraḍa)," as the poet said [[The poet is Labid. The meaning of the verse: when a kindness is done to you, repay it in kind.]]:

"And when you are repaid with a loan, repay it, for only the noble man repays, not the camel."

It is called a loan (qarḍ) because a loan is given out in order to recover its equivalent; that is, "Who is it that will spend in the way of Allah so that Allah replaces it with many multiples?" Al-Kalbi said: "a loan (qarḍan)" means charity, "goodly (ḥasanan)" means seeking reward from the heart, without reproach or injury.

﴿So He may multiply it for him﴾: between seven and seven hundred, and beyond that by whatever multiples Allah wills. It has also been said: the goodly loan is to say, "Subḥān Allāh, al-ḥamdu lillāh, lā ilāha illā Allāh, and Allāhu akbar." This was narrated by Sufyan from Abu Ḥayyān [[All copies of the original read Abu Ḥayyān, but the correct reading is apparently Ibn Ḥayyān.]]. Zayd ibn Aslam said: it is spending on one's family. Al-Ḥasan said: it is voluntary acts of worship. It has also been said: it is doing good deeds, and the Arabs say: "I have a loan of sincerity (qarḍ ṣidq) with so-and-so, and a loan of evil (qarḍ sū')." Al-Qushayri said: the goodly loan is that the giver be sincere in intention and content of heart, seeking the Face of Allah without showing off or seeking reputation, and that it be from what is lawful. Among the goodly loan is that one not intend the bad and give it, due to His saying: ﴿and do not aim at the bad to spend from it﴾ [[See vol. 3 p. 325]]; and that one give charity in a state where one still hopes for life, for the Prophet ﷺ was asked about the best charity and he said: "That you give while you are healthy and miserly, hoping for wealth, and do not delay until, when the throat rattles, you say: 'To so-and-so such-and-such, and to so-and-so such-and-such.'" And that one conceal one's charity, due to His saying: ﴿And if you conceal it and give it to the poor, it is better for you﴾ [[See vol. 3 p. 332 and p. (311)]]; and that one not bestow reproach, due to His saying: ﴿Do not nullify your charities with reproach and injury﴾ [[See vol. 3 p. 332 and p. (311)]]; and that one consider little whatever one gives, because the whole world is little; and that it be from one's most beloved wealth, due to His saying: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend of what you love﴾ [[See vol. 4 p. 132]]; and that it be abundant, due to the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The best slaves to free are the most costly in price and the most precious to their owners."

﴿So He may multiply it for him﴾: Ibn Kathir and Ibn ʿAmir read (fa-yuḍaʿʿifahu) without the alif, except that Ibn ʿAmir and Yaʿqub put the fa' in the accusative. Nafi' and the people of Kufa and Basra read (fa-yuḍāʿifahu) with the alif and a light ʿayn, except that ʿAsim put the fa' in the accusative. The rest read it in the nominative, as a conjunction to (yuqriḍu), and in the accusative as an answer to the interrogative. The discussion of this has been fully treated in (al-Baqarah) [[See vol. 3 p. 332 and p. (311)]].

﴿And he will have a generous reward﴾: meaning Paradise.

Allah Almighty says: ﴿On the day you see the believing men and believing women﴾: the governing element of (yawma, "on the day") is (and he will have a generous reward). In the sentence there is an ellipsis, i.e., (and he will have a generous reward) on the day you see (the believing men and believing women), their light running (yasʿā nūruhum) — that is, passing over the Ṣirāṭ according to al-Ḥasan — which is the light by which they pass, (before them) — that is, in front of them.

(And on their right hands): al-Farra' said: the bāʾ means "in" — that is, in their right hands; or it means "from," that is, from their right hands. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: (their light) is their guidance, and (on their right hands) are their books. Al-Ṭabarī preferred this: their faith and righteous deeds run before them, and in their right hands are the books of their deeds. The bāʾ on this view means "in." It is permissible on this view to pause at (before them), and not to pause if it means "from." Sahl ibn Saʿd al-Saʿidi and Abu Ḥaywa read (wa-bi-aymānihim) with a kasra on the alif, meaning the faith which is the opposite of disbelief.

He coordinated what is not an adverbial phrase with the adverbial phrase, because the meaning of the adverbial phrase is a state, and it is attached to an ellipsis. The meaning is: running, being (before them) and being (on their right hands); and his saying (before them) is not attached to (yasʿā) itself. It has also been said: by the light he meant the Qur'an. It is narrated from Ibn Masʿud: they are given their light according to the measure of their deeds; among them is one whose light is given like a palm tree, and among them one whose light is given like a standing man, and the least of them in light is one whose light is on the toe of his foot, flickering once and kindled another time. Qatada said: it was mentioned to us that the Prophet of Allah ﷺ said: "Among the believers is one whose light shines as far as between Medina and Aden, or between Medina and Sanaa, and even beyond that, until there is one whose light shines only on the place of his two feet." Al-Ḥasan said: so that they may be guided by it over the Ṣirāṭ, as previously mentioned. Muqatil said: so that it may be a guide for them to Paradise. And Allah knows best.

Allah Almighty says: ﴿Good news for you today: gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾. The estimated sense: it will be said to them, "Good news for you today: entry into gardens." It is necessary to estimate an omitted genitive, because good news is an event, while the Garden is a substance, so the one cannot be the other.

(Beneath which rivers flow): that is, beneath them flow rivers of milk, water, wine and honey from beneath their dwellings.

(Abiding therein): a state of the omitted entry, the estimate being: "Good news for you today: entry into gardens (beneath which rivers flow), (while) abiding therein." The state should not be from "your good news," because that would separate the relative clause from the relative pronoun. It is permissible that it be what is indicated by "good news," as if he said: "You are given good news, abiding." It is also permissible that the adverb "today," which is "today," be the predicate of "your good news," and "gardens" be an apposition to "good news" on the estimate of the omitted genitive, as previously mentioned. "Abiding" is a state according to what has preceded. Al-Farra' permitted the accusative of "gardens" as a state, with "today" being the predicate of "your good news," but this is far-fetched, since "gardens" contains no sense of a verb. He also permitted "your good news" to be in the accusative, meaning "they give them good news, a good news," with "gardens" governed by "good news," but this involves separating the relative clause from the relative pronoun.

The Quranic phrase ﴿On the Day when the hypocrite men and women say to the believers﴾: what governs "the Day" (yawma) is "That is the great triumph" (ﷻ). It is also said that it is a substitute (badal) for the first "Day."

(Look upon us, that we may borrow from your light): the common reading (qira'ah) has a connected alif, with the zay vowelled with a damma, from naẓara, and naẓar here means waiting, i.e., "wait for us." Al-A'mash, Hamzah and Yahya ibn Wathhab read (unẓurūnā) with a cut alif and a kasra on the ẓā', from al-inẓār, meaning "give us respite and delay us." It is said: anẓartuhu, I delayed him; and istanẓartuhu, I asked him for a respite. Al-Farra' said: the Arabs say anẓirnī, meaning "wait for me." He cited the verse of 'Amr ibn Kulthum:

"Abu Hind, do not hurry against us,
and wait for us, we will inform you with certainty,"

meaning, "wait for us."

(That we may borrow from your light): i.e., that we may take light from your light. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Umamah said: a darkness covers people on the Day of Resurrection. Al-Mawardi said: I think this is after the judgement has been concluded. Then they are given a light by which they walk. The exegetes said: Allah gives the believers a light on the Day of Resurrection according to the measure of their deeds, by which they walk over the Sirat (bridge). He also gives the hypocrites a light, as a deception to them. The proof is His saying ﴿And He is their deceiver﴾ (See vol. 5, p. 421). It is also said: they are given light only because all of them are people of the call (da'wah), unlike the disbeliever. Then the hypocrite's light is taken away because of his hypocrisy; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. Abu Umamah said: the believer is given light, and the disbeliever and the hypocrite are left without light. Al-Kalbi said: rather, the hypocrites borrow light from the believers and are not given light. Then, while they are walking, Allah sends a wind and darkness upon them, and this extinguishes the hypocrites' light. That is His saying ﴿Our Lord, perfect for us our light﴾ (See vol. 7, p. 211), which the believers say out of fear that it will be taken from them as it was taken from the hypocrites. When the hypocrites remain in darkness, not seeing the places of their feet, they say to the believers: (Look upon us, that we may borrow from your light).

(It will be said: Go back behind you): i.e., the angels said to them: "Go back." It is also said: rather, it is the believers' saying to them: "Go back behind you," to the place from which we took the light; so seek there a light for yourselves, for you will not borrow from our light. When they returned and withdrew to seek light, (a wall was set up between them). It is also said: meaning, why did you not seek the light from the world, by believing?

(with a wall): i.e., a wall (sūr), and the bā' is extra (ṣilah). Al-Kisa'i said this. The wall is a barrier between Paradise and Hell. It is narrated that this wall is at Bayt al-Maqdis, near a place known as the Valley of Hell (Wādī Jahannam).

(Its inner side has mercy in it): i.e., the side that is toward the believers. (And its outer side, facing it, is punishment): i.e., the side that is toward the hypocrites. Ka'b al-Ahbar said: it is the gate in Bayt al-Maqdis known as the Gate of Mercy. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr said: it is the eastern wall of Bayt al-Maqdis; its inner side has the mosque in it. (And its outer side, facing it, is punishment): i.e., Hell. Similar was reported from Ibn 'Abbas. Ziyad ibn Abi Sawda said: 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit stood on the eastern wall of Bayt al-Maqdis and wept, and said: "From here the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) told us that he saw Hell." Qatadah said: it is a wall between Paradise and Hell. (Its inner side has mercy in it): i.e., Paradise. (And its outer side, facing it, is punishment): i.e., Hell. Mujahid said: it is a partition (ḥijāb), as in (al-A'raf), and its matter has been discussed there (See vol. 7, p. 211). It has been said that the mercy within it is the light of the believers, and the punishment on its outside is the darkness of the hypocrites.

The Quranic phrase ﴿They will call out to them﴾: i.e., the hypocrites will call out to the believers: (Were we not with you?): in the world, meaning: we prayed as you pray, we fought as you fight, and we did as you do. (They will say, "Yes"): i.e., the believers will say: (Yes), you were indeed with us outwardly. (But you led yourselves into temptation): i.e., you used yourselves for temptation. Mujahid said: you destroyed yourselves through hypocrisy. It is also said: through sins; this was said by Abu Sinan. It is also said: through desires and pleasures; this was narrated by Abu Numayr al-Hamdani.

(You waited and doubted): i.e., you waited for the Prophet (ﷺ) to die, and for the believers to suffer calamities. It is also said: you waited to repent (tawbah). (And you doubted): i.e., you were skeptical about monotheism and prophethood. (And false hopes deceived you): i.e., the falsehoods (al-abātīl). It is also said: the lengthening of hope. It is also said: it is what they wished for, that the believers would be weakened and calamities would descend upon them. Qatadah said: the "false hopes" here are the deceptions of Satan. It is also said: the world; this was said by 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas (in MSS b, z, s, l, h: 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ayyash). Abu Sinan said: it is their saying, "We will be forgiven." Bilal ibn Sa'd said: remembering your good deeds while forgetting your bad deeds is delusion.

(Until the command of Allah came): i.e., death. It is also said: the victory of His Prophet (ﷺ). Qatadah said: their being cast into the Fire.

(And the Deceiver deceived you about Allah): i.e., deceived you. (Al-Gharur): i.e., Satan; this was said by 'Ikrimah. It is also said: the world; this was said by al-Dahhak. Some scholars said: for the one who remains, there is a lesson in the one who has passed; and for the one who is later, there is a restraint from the one who came first. The fortunate one is he who is not deceived by greed, and does not lean toward deceptions. Whoever remembers death forgets wishful thinking; whoever prolongs hope forgets action and neglects the appointed term. The word (al-Gharur) is in the intensive form (mubālagah), indicating abundance. Abu Haywah, Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa' and Simak ibn Harb read (al-Ghurur) with a damma on the ghayn, meaning falsehoods, and it is a verbal noun (maṣdar). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) drew lines for us, and drew one line to one side, and said: "Do you know what this is? This is the son of Adam, and this is the wish (tamannī), and those lines are the hopes, while he is wishing, when death comes to him." It is also reported from Ibn Mas'ud who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) drew for us a square, and drew a line in its middle extending outside it, and drew small lines to its right and left, and said: "This is the son of Adam, and this is his term encompassing him, and this is his hope, which has exceeded his term, and these small lines are the calamities. If this one misses him, that one bites him, and if that one misses him, this one bites him."

The Quranic phrase: ﴿So on that Day no ransom will be taken from you﴾, O hypocrites, ﴿nor from those who disbelieved﴾: i.e., they are despaired of salvation. The common reading is (yu'khadhu) with a yā', because the feminine is not real (ḥaqīqī), and because a separation has come between it and the verb. Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read (tu'khadhu) with a tā', and Abu Hatim chose it because fidyah (ransom) is feminine. The first is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd. That is, no substitute, compensation, or other soul will be accepted from you.

(Your abode is the Fire): i.e., your place of stay and dwelling. (It is your protector): i.e., more fitting for you. The mawlā is one who manages a person's affairs, and then it was used for one who is constantly attached to a thing. **Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 57, verses 16–17:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe﴾, meaning: has it not drawn near and become due? The poet said:

Has the time not come for me, O heart, to abandon ignorance,
and for the manifest white hair to make us wise?

Its past tense is *anā* (أنى), with the final vowel shortened, *yaʾnī* in the present. It is also said: *āna laka* (آنَ لَكَ), with the long vowel, *an tafʿala kadhā yaʾīnu aynan*, meaning *ḥāna* (it has become due), like *anā laka* (أنى لك), and it is an inversion of it. Ibn al-Sikkit recited:

Has it not yet come for me that my blindness be cleared,
and that I refrain from Layla? Yes, it has come to me.

Thus he combined the two dialects. Al-Hasan recited *ʾalammā yaʾni* (ألَمَّا يَأْنِ), and its original form is *ʾalam*, with *mā* added. *Mā* negates the speaker's statement "it has already been so," while *lam* negates his statement "it was so."

In Sahih Muslim, it is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "The time between our conversion to Islam and the moment God rebuked us with this verse, ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of God﴾, was only four years."

Al-Khalil said: *al-ʿitāb* (العتاب, reproach) is address made with familiarity and a recalling of resentment. One says: *ʿātabtuhu muʿātabatan* (عاتبته معاتبة). ﴿That they should humble themselves﴾ means that they should become submissive and soft. ﴿Their hearts to the remembrance of God and what has descended of the truth﴾.

It is related that jesting and laughter became frequent among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ when they lived in comfort in Medina, and so this verse was revealed. When this verse was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ said: "God is calling you slow to humility." At that they said: "We have humbled ourselves."

Ibn ʿAbbas said: God found the hearts of the believers slow, so He rebuked them thirteen years after the beginning of the revelation of the Qur'an.

It is also said that it was revealed about the hypocrites one year after the Hijra. They had asked Salman to tell them the wonders of the Torah, and then the verses were revealed: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Book that makes things clear﴾ [see vol. 9, p. 118], up to His saying: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾. He informed them that this narrative was better than others and more beneficial for them. So they desisted from Salman. Then they asked him again in the same way, and this verse was revealed: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of God and what has descended of the truth?﴾ According to this interpretation, ﴿those who believe﴾ refers to belief outwardly, in speech.

Al-Suddi and others said: ﴿Those who believe﴾ refers to those who appear to believe while concealing disbelief, and the verse means ﴿that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of God﴾.

It is also said that it was revealed about the believers. Sa'd said: It was said, "O Messenger of God, if you were to relate stories to us," and then the verse was revealed: ﴿We relate to you﴾. Then after a time they said, "If only you would speak to us," and the verse was revealed: ﴿God has sent down the best of speech﴾ [see vol. 15, p. 248]. Then after a period they said, "If only you would admonish us," and God the Exalted revealed: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of God and what has descended of the truth?﴾

Similar is related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The time between our conversion to Islam and the moment we were rebuked with this verse was only four years." Then each of us began looking at the others and saying, "What have we done anew?"

Al-Hasan said: He found them slow, though they were the most beloved of His creation to Him.

It is also said that this address is to those who believed in Moses and Jesus, not Muhammad, peace be upon them, because after this He said: ﴿And those who believe in God and His messengers﴾. That is: has the time not come for those who believed in the Torah and the Gospel that their hearts should soften to the Qur'an, and that they should not be like the earlier people of Moses and Jesus, for the term grew long between them and their prophet, and so their hearts hardened.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that they should not be﴾, meaning: and that they should not be. It is in the accusative, coordinated with ﴿that their hearts should humble themselves﴾. It is also said that it is in the jussive, governed by the prohibition, its sense being: "And let them not be." The evidence for this interpretation is the transmission of Ruways from Yaʿqub, reading *lā takūnū* (لا تكونوا) with a *tāʾ*, which is the reading of ʿIsā and Ibn Ishaq. It means: do not follow the path of the Jews and the Christians, who were given the Torah and the Gospel, but the ages grew long for them.

Ibn Mas'ud said: When the Children of Israel's term grew long, their hearts hardened. They invented a book of their own, which their souls found lawful, and the truth had been preventing them from many of their desires. Until they cast the Book of God behind their backs as if they did not know. Then they said: "Present this book to the Children of Israel. If they follow you, leave them alone, but otherwise kill them." Then they agreed to send it to one of their scholars, and they said: "If he follows us, no one will oppose us, and if he refuses we will kill him, and no one will dispute with us after him." So they sent to him. He wrote the Book of God on a sheet, placed it in a horn [the addition is from Tafsir al-Tabari], hung it on his neck, and then put his clothes over it. He came to them, and they presented their book to him and said: "Do you believe in this?" He struck his hand on his chest and said: "I believe in this," meaning what was hung on his chest. Then the Children of Israel split into seventy-odd sects, and the best of their sects were the people of Dhu al-Qarnayn.

ʿAbd Allah said: "Whoever among you lives will see what is evil, and it is enough for one of you, when he sees evil and cannot change it, that God knows from his heart that he hates it."

Muqatil ibn Hayyan [in some tafsirs: Muqatil ibn Sulayman, who is the commentator] said: It means the believers among the People of the Book, the term grew long for them, and they were slow to await the sending of the Prophet ﷺ. ﴿So their hearts hardened, and many of them are defiant﴾, meaning those who innovated monasticism, the people of the monasteries. It is also said: they are those who do not know the religion they practise in jurisprudence, and who oppose those who know. It is also said: they are those who will not believe in the knowledge of God the Exalted. A group of them remained upon the religion of Jesus until the Prophet ﷺ was sent, and they believed in him, while another group of them turned away from the religion of Jesus, and they are those whom God declared defiant.

Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: The Companions were in Mecca in hardship, but when they emigrated they found abundance and blessing, and so they slackened from what they had been doing, their hearts hardened, and God admonished them, and they awoke.

Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned: Malik ibn Anas informed us, saying: It reached me that Jesus, peace be upon him, said to his people: "Do not multiply speech without the remembrance of God the Exalted, lest your hearts harden, for the hard heart is far from God, but you do not know it. Do not look into the sins of people as if you were lords, but look into them, or he said, into your own sins, as if you were servants. For people are of two kinds: the one who is healthy and the one who is afflicted. So have mercy on the people of affliction, and praise God for well-being."

This verse, ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of God﴾, was the cause of the repentance of al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad and Ibn al-Mubarak, may God have mercy on them both.

Abu al-Mutarrif ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Marwan al-Qalansi mentioned, saying: Abu Muhammad al-Hasan ibn Rashiq related to us, saying: ʿAli ibn Yaʿqub al-Zayyat related to us, saying: Ibrahim ibn Hisham related to us, saying: Zakariyya ibn Abi Aban related to us, saying: al-Layth ibn al-Harith related to us, saying: al-Hasan ibn Dahir related to us, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mubarak was asked about the beginning of his asceticism (*zuhd*, renunciation of worldly pleasures). He said: "One day I was with my brothers in an orchard of ours, at the time when the fruit trees bore various kinds of fruit. We ate and drank until night, then we slept. I was devoted to playing the lute and the *ṭunbūr*. In the middle of the night I got up and played with a voice called Rashin [the name is as it stands in the manuscripts, and we have not found it after searching] of the dawn, and Sinan wanted to sing, and a bird was crying out over my head on a tree. The lute was in my hand and did not answer me to what I wanted. Suddenly it spoke as a human speaks, that is, the lute in my hand, and it said: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of God and what has descended of the truth?﴾ I said: 'Yes, by God!' and I broke the lute, and I dismissed those who were with me. This was the first of my asceticism and my resolve."

We have also been informed of the verse that Ibn al-Mubarak wanted to sing to the lute:

Has it not come for me, from you, that you show mercy,
and disregard the blamers and the reproachers?

And that you pity a lover, enamoured of you,
who has kept mourning over your separation?

He spends the night, when his night covers him,
watching the stars and the constellations.

And what harm would it be for the gazelle, if it
were permitted to share in union what it had forbidden?

As for al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad, the cause of his repentance was that he fell in love with a slave girl, and she promised him a meeting at night. While he was climbing the walls toward her, he heard a reciter reading: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of God?﴾ He turned back, saying: "Yes, by God, it has come!" Then the night sheltered him in a ruin where a group of travellers were, and some of them were saying to others: "Fudayl is a highway robber." Al-Fudayl said: "Alas! Do I go out at night to disobey God? People of the Muslims are afraid of me! O God, I have repented to You, and I make my repentance to You the neighbourhood of Your Sacred House."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Know that God gives life to the earth after its death﴾, meaning: ﴿He gives life to the earth﴾ that is barren ﴿after its death﴾ through rain. It is also said: the meaning is that in the same way God gives life to the disbeliever with guidance to faith after his death through disbelief and error. It is also said: in the same way God gives life to the dead of the nations, and distinguishes between the one whose heart is humble and the one whose heart is hard.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 57, verses 16–17:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe﴾, meaning: has it not drawn near and become due? The poet said:

Has the time not come for me, O heart, to abandon ignorance,
and for the manifest white hair to make us wise?

Its past tense is *anā* (أنى), with the final vowel shortened, *yaʾnī* in the present. It is also said: *āna laka* (آنَ لَكَ), with the long vowel, *an tafʿala kadhā yaʾīnu aynan*, meaning *ḥāna* (it has become due), like *anā laka* (أنى لك), and it is an inversion of it. Ibn al-Sikkit recited:

Has it not yet come for me that my blindness be cleared,
and that I refrain from Layla? Yes, it has come to me.

Thus he combined the two dialects. Al-Hasan recited *ʾalammā yaʾni* (ألَمَّا يَأْنِ), and its original form is *ʾalam*, with *mā* added. *Mā* negates the speaker's statement "it has already been so," while *lam* negates his statement "it was so."

In Sahih Muslim, it is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "The time between our conversion to Islam and the moment God rebuked us with this verse, ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of God﴾, was only four years."

Al-Khalil said: *al-ʿitāb* (العتاب, reproach) is address made with familiarity and a recalling of resentment. One says: *ʿātabtuhu muʿātabatan* (عاتبته معاتبة). ﴿That they should humble themselves﴾ means that they should become submissive and soft. ﴿Their hearts to the remembrance of God and what has descended of the truth﴾.

It is related that jesting and laughter became frequent among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ when they lived in comfort in Medina, and so this verse was revealed. When this verse was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ said: "God is calling you slow to humility." At that they said: "We have humbled ourselves."

Ibn ʿAbbas said: God found the hearts of the believers slow, so He rebuked them thirteen years after the beginning of the revelation of the Qur'an.

It is also said that it was revealed about the hypocrites one year after the Hijra. They had asked Salman to tell them the wonders of the Torah, and then the verses were revealed: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Book that makes things clear﴾ [see vol. 9, p. 118], up to His saying: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories﴾. He informed them that this narrative was better than others and more beneficial for them. So they desisted from Salman. Then they asked him again in the same way, and this verse was revealed: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of God and what has descended of the truth?﴾ According to this interpretation, ﴿those who believe﴾ refers to belief outwardly, in speech.

Al-Suddi and others said: ﴿Those who believe﴾ refers to those who appear to believe while concealing disbelief, and the verse means ﴿that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of God﴾.

It is also said that it was revealed about the believers. Sa'd said: It was said, "O Messenger of God, if you were to relate stories to us," and then the verse was revealed: ﴿We relate to you﴾. Then after a time they said, "If only you would speak to us," and the verse was revealed: ﴿God has sent down the best of speech﴾ [see vol. 15, p. 248]. Then after a period they said, "If only you would admonish us," and God the Exalted revealed: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of God and what has descended of the truth?﴾

Similar is related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The time between our conversion to Islam and the moment we were rebuked with this verse was only four years." Then each of us began looking at the others and saying, "What have we done anew?"

Al-Hasan said: He found them slow, though they were the most beloved of His creation to Him.

It is also said that this address is to those who believed in Moses and Jesus, not Muhammad, peace be upon them, because after this He said: ﴿And those who believe in God and His messengers﴾. That is: has the time not come for those who believed in the Torah and the Gospel that their hearts should soften to the Qur'an, and that they should not be like the earlier people of Moses and Jesus, for the term grew long between them and their prophet, and so their hearts hardened.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that they should not be﴾, meaning: and that they should not be. It is in the accusative, coordinated with ﴿that their hearts should humble themselves﴾. It is also said that it is in the jussive, governed by the prohibition, its sense being: "And let them not be." The evidence for this interpretation is the transmission of Ruways from Yaʿqub, reading *lā takūnū* (لا تكونوا) with a *tāʾ*, which is the reading of ʿIsā and Ibn Ishaq. It means: do not follow the path of the Jews and the Christians, who were given the Torah and the Gospel, but the ages grew long for them.

Ibn Mas'ud said: When the Children of Israel's term grew long, their hearts hardened. They invented a book of their own, which their souls found lawful, and the truth had been preventing them from many of their desires. Until they cast the Book of God behind their backs as if they did not know. Then they said: "Present this book to the Children of Israel. If they follow you, leave them alone, but otherwise kill them." Then they agreed to send it to one of their scholars, and they said: "If he follows us, no one will oppose us, and if he refuses we will kill him, and no one will dispute with us after him." So they sent to him. He wrote the Book of God on a sheet, placed it in a horn [the addition is from Tafsir al-Tabari], hung it on his neck, and then put his clothes over it. He came to them, and they presented their book to him and said: "Do you believe in this?" He struck his hand on his chest and said: "I believe in this," meaning what was hung on his chest. Then the Children of Israel split into seventy-odd sects, and the best of their sects were the people of Dhu al-Qarnayn.

ʿAbd Allah said: "Whoever among you lives will see what is evil, and it is enough for one of you, when he sees evil and cannot change it, that God knows from his heart that he hates it."

Muqatil ibn Hayyan [in some tafsirs: Muqatil ibn Sulayman, who is the commentator] said: It means the believers among the People of the Book, the term grew long for them, and they were slow to await the sending of the Prophet ﷺ. ﴿So their hearts hardened, and many of them are defiant﴾, meaning those who innovated monasticism, the people of the monasteries. It is also said: they are those who do not know the religion they practise in jurisprudence, and who oppose those who know. It is also said: they are those who will not believe in the knowledge of God the Exalted. A group of them remained upon the religion of Jesus until the Prophet ﷺ was sent, and they believed in him, while another group of them turned away from the religion of Jesus, and they are those whom God declared defiant.

Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: The Companions were in Mecca in hardship, but when they emigrated they found abundance and blessing, and so they slackened from what they had been doing, their hearts hardened, and God admonished them, and they awoke.

Ibn al-Mubarak mentioned: Malik ibn Anas informed us, saying: It reached me that Jesus, peace be upon him, said to his people: "Do not multiply speech without the remembrance of God the Exalted, lest your hearts harden, for the hard heart is far from God, but you do not know it. Do not look into the sins of people as if you were lords, but look into them, or he said, into your own sins, as if you were servants. For people are of two kinds: the one who is healthy and the one who is afflicted. So have mercy on the people of affliction, and praise God for well-being."

This verse, ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of God﴾, was the cause of the repentance of al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad and Ibn al-Mubarak, may God have mercy on them both.

Abu al-Mutarrif ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Marwan al-Qalansi mentioned, saying: Abu Muhammad al-Hasan ibn Rashiq related to us, saying: ʿAli ibn Yaʿqub al-Zayyat related to us, saying: Ibrahim ibn Hisham related to us, saying: Zakariyya ibn Abi Aban related to us, saying: al-Layth ibn al-Harith related to us, saying: al-Hasan ibn Dahir related to us, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Mubarak was asked about the beginning of his asceticism (*zuhd*, renunciation of worldly pleasures). He said: "One day I was with my brothers in an orchard of ours, at the time when the fruit trees bore various kinds of fruit. We ate and drank until night, then we slept. I was devoted to playing the lute and the *ṭunbūr*. In the middle of the night I got up and played with a voice called Rashin [the name is as it stands in the manuscripts, and we have not found it after searching] of the dawn, and Sinan wanted to sing, and a bird was crying out over my head on a tree. The lute was in my hand and did not answer me to what I wanted. Suddenly it spoke as a human speaks, that is, the lute in my hand, and it said: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of God and what has descended of the truth?﴾ I said: 'Yes, by God!' and I broke the lute, and I dismissed those who were with me. This was the first of my asceticism and my resolve."

We have also been informed of the verse that Ibn al-Mubarak wanted to sing to the lute:

Has it not come for me, from you, that you show mercy,
and disregard the blamers and the reproachers?

And that you pity a lover, enamoured of you,
who has kept mourning over your separation?

He spends the night, when his night covers him,
watching the stars and the constellations.

And what harm would it be for the gazelle, if it
were permitted to share in union what it had forbidden?

As for al-Fudayl ibn ʿIyad, the cause of his repentance was that he fell in love with a slave girl, and she promised him a meeting at night. While he was climbing the walls toward her, he heard a reciter reading: ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of God?﴾ He turned back, saying: "Yes, by God, it has come!" Then the night sheltered him in a ruin where a group of travellers were, and some of them were saying to others: "Fudayl is a highway robber." Al-Fudayl said: "Alas! Do I go out at night to disobey God? People of the Muslims are afraid of me! O God, I have repented to You, and I make my repentance to You the neighbourhood of Your Sacred House."

Salih al-Murri said: the meaning is that He softens hearts after their hardness. Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad said: He gives them life through justice after injustice. It is also said: the meaning is that in the same way God gives life to the disbeliever with guidance to faith after his death through disbelief and error. It is also said: in the same way God gives life to the dead of the nations, and distinguishes between the one whose heart is humble and the one whose heart is hard.

﴿We have indeed made the signs clear to you, so that you may understand﴾, meaning: God's giving life to the earth after its death is evidence of God's power, and that He is indeed the one who gives life to the dead.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 57, verse 18–19:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the men who give charity and the women who give charity﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr, on the authority of ʿAsim, read the ṣād in both words with a light doubling, from taṣdīq (affirmation), meaning "those who affirm what Allah has sent down." The rest read it with the doubling (shaddah), meaning al-mutaṣaddiqīn and al-mutaṣaddiqāt, and the tāʾ was assimilated into the ṣād. It is likewise in the codex of Ubayy. This is an exhortation to give charity, and for this reason He says: (and lend to Allah a goodly loan), by charity and spending in the way of Allah. Al-Hasan said: whatever in the Qur'an is "a goodly loan" is voluntary giving. It was also said: it is righteous deed, including charity and other things, done sincerely seeking reward. The verb is coordinated with the noun because that noun carries the sense of a verb, meaning: indeed those who gave charity and lent to Allah, (it will be multiplied for them), and theirs is a multiplication. The common reading is with a fatḥah on the ʿayn, in the passive form (lam yusamma fāʿiluh, the agent unnamed). Al-Aʿmash read (yuḍāʿifuhu) with a kasrah on the ʿayn and an added hāʾ. Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʿAmir and Yaʿqub read (yuḍaʿʿafu) with a fatḥah on the ʿayn and a doubling of it.

(And for them is a noble reward), meaning Paradise.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And those who believed in Allah and His messengers, they are the ṣiddīqūn (truthful ones) and the shuhadāʾ (martyrs/witnesses) with their Lord; for them is their reward and their light﴾. It is disputed whether (al-shuhadāʾ) is separate from what precedes it or connected to it. Mujahid and Zayd ibn Aslam said: the shuhadāʾ and the ṣiddīqīn are the believers, and it is connected; its meaning is related from the Prophet ﷺ, so one does not pause at His words "al-ṣiddīqūn." This is also the view of Ibn Masʿud regarding the interpretation of the verse. Al-Qushayri said: Allah the Exalted said: (So those will be with those whom Allah has blessed of the prophets, the ṣiddīqīn, the shuhadāʾ and the righteous) [see vol. 5 p. 271 and p. 197]. So the ṣiddīqūn are those who follow the prophets, the shuhadāʾ are those who follow the ṣiddīqīn, and the righteous follow the shuhadāʾ. It is therefore possible that this verse concerns all who affirmed the messengers, namely (And those who believed in Allah and His messengers, they are the ṣiddīqūn and the shuhadāʾ). The shuhadāʾ here would be those who bore witness to Allah's oneness, so there is a ṣiddīq above a ṣiddīq in rank, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed the people of the high gardens are seen by those below them as one sees the star that is on the horizon of the sky, and indeed Abu Bakr and ʿUmar are among them, and they are blessed."

It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and Masruq that the shuhadāʾ are other than the ṣiddīqīn. On this view, al-shuhadāʾ is separate from what precedes it, and the pause at His words "al-ṣiddīqūn" is good. The meaning: and the shuhadāʾ with their Lord; for them is their reward and their light, i.e., for them is the reward of their own selves and the light of their own selves. Regarding them there are two opinions. The first: they are the messengers, who testify against their peoples with regard to affirmation and denial; this is said by al-Kalbi, and its evidence is His statement: (And We bring you as a witness against these) [see vol. 5 p. 271 and p. 197]. The second: they are the communities of the messengers who testify on the Day of Resurrection. Concerning what they testify, there are two views. One: they testify against themselves regarding what they did of obedience and disobedience; this is the meaning of Mujahid's view. The second: they testify on behalf of their prophets regarding their conveying the message to their peoples; this is said by al-Kalbi. Muqatil stated a third view: they are those slain in the way of Allah. Similar is related from Ibn ʿAbbas as well, who said: he meant the martyrs among the believers. The waw here is the waw of beginning (resumption). And the ṣiddīqūn on this view are separated from the shuhadāʾ.

It has been disputed concerning their identity. al-Dahhak said: they are eight men: Abu Bakr, ʿAli, Zayd, ʿUthman, Talhah, al-Zubayr, Saʿd and Hamzah. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab followed them, may Allah be pleased with them all; Allah joined him to them when he affirmed His Prophet ﷺ. Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: the ṣiddīqūn are those who believed in the messengers and did not deny them for the blink of an eye, such as the believer of the family of Pharaoh, the companion of the family of Yasin, Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, and the people of the trench.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs﴾, i.e., the messengers and the miracles, (they are the companions of the Blazing Fire), so for them there is neither reward nor light.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 57, verse 20–21:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Know that the life of this world is only play and amusement﴾. The connection (wajh al-ittisal) is that a person may abandon jihad out of fear for his own self from being killed, and out of fear of the inevitability of death. So He made clear that the life of this world is transient, and it is not fitting that the command of God be abandoned in order to preserve what does not endure. The "ma" (ma) is redundant (sila); its implied meaning is: Know that the life of this world is vain play and amusement of joy, then it comes to an end. Qatada said: "Play and amusement: eating and drinking." It was also said that it is according to its well-known meaning. Mujahid said: "Every play is amusement." This meaning has already passed in (al-An'am) [[See vol. 6, p. 414]]. It was also said: play is what makes one desire the world, and amusement is what diverts one from the Hereafter, i.e., preoccupies one from it. It was also said: play is acquisition (ightina'), and amusement is women.

(And adornment) zina is what one adorns oneself with. The disbeliever adorns himself with the world and does not work for the Hereafter, and likewise whoever adorns himself in disobedience to God.

(And boasting among you) i.e., some of you boast over others with it. It was said: with creation and strength. It was said: with lineage, according to the Arab custom of boasting about fathers. In Sahih Muslim, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he said: "God revealed to me that you should be humble, so that no one oppresses another and no one boasts over another." It is also authentically reported from him, peace be upon him, that he said: "Four matters from the affairs of the Jahiliyyah remain in my community: boasting about lineage..." the hadith. All of this has already passed.

(And competition in wealth and children) because the custom of the Jahiliyyah was to compete in sons and wealth, while the competition of the believers is in faith and obedience. Some later scholars said: (play) like the play of children, (amusement) like the amusement of youths, (adornment) like the adornment of women, (boasting) like the boasting of peers, (competition) like the competition of the dihqan [[al-dihqan – with the dal vowelled either way: a merchant, a Persian word arabized.]]. It was also said: the meaning is that the world is like these things in passing away and perishing. It is reported from Ali, may God be pleased with him, that he said to Ammar: "Do not grieve over the world, for the world consists of six things: food, drink, clothing, scent, mount, and marriage. The best of its food is honey, which is the spittle of a fly; its most abundant drink is water, shared by all animals; its finest clothing is brocade, which is the weaving of a worm; its finest scent is musk, which is the blood of a mouse; its finest mount is the horse, and upon it men are killed; as for marriage, it is women, which is 'a discharge into a discharge'. By God, a woman adorns her best so that her worst is desired."

Then God struck a parable for it with crops after rain, saying: (like rain) i.e., a downpour, (whose growth pleases the disbelievers). Here "the disbelievers" means the farmers, because they cover the seed [[derived from kufr, with fatha on the kaf, meaning covering]]. The meaning is that the life of this world is like crops that please those who look at them for their greenery due to abundant rain, then soon it becomes stubble as if it had never been. When it pleases the farmers, it is the utmost of what is admired. The meaning of this parable has already passed in (Yunus) [[See vol. 8, p. 327]] and (al-Kahf) [[See vol. 10, p. 412]]. It was also said: "the disbelievers" here means those who disbelieve in God, the Mighty and Majestic, because they are more pleased with the adornment of the world than the believers. This is a good view, for the root of pleasure belongs to them and in them, and from them it appears, namely the glorifying of the world and what is in it. Among the monotheists there are branches of this that arise from their desires, and they diminish in their eyes and become small when they remember the Hereafter. The place of the kaf is in the nominative as an adjective.

(Then it withers) i.e., dries after its greenness, (then you see it turned yellow) i.e., changed from the freshness it had been.

(Then it becomes debris) i.e., crumbs and chaff, and it goes away after its beauty; so too is the world of the disbeliever.

(And in the Hereafter there is severe punishment) i.e., for the disbelievers. It is good to pause here, and then begin: (and forgiveness from God and good pleasure) i.e., for the believers. Al-Farra' said: "(And in the Hereafter there is severe punishment and forgiveness)" its meaning is either severe punishment or forgiveness, so one does not pause at "severe."

(And the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion.) This is an emphasis of what preceded: it deceives the disbelievers; as for the believer, the world is for him a provision that reaches to Paradise. It was also said: working for the life of this world is "the enjoyment of delusion," as a discouragement from working for the world and an encouragement to working for the Hereafter.

(Except that it is in a Book) meaning in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

(Before We bring it into being) The pronoun in (nabra'aha) refers to the souls, or the earth, or the calamities, or all of them. Ibn Abbas said: before He creates the calamity. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: before He creates the earth and the soul.

Al-Rabi' ibn Salih said: When Sa'id ibn Jubayr, may Allah be pleased with him, was seized, I wept. He said: "What makes you weep?" I said: "I weep for what I see of you and for what you are heading towards." He said: "Do not weep, for it was in Allah's knowledge that it would happen. Have you not heard His saying, Exalted is He: (No calamity befalls on earth or in yourselves) to the end of the verse?" Ibn Abbas said: When Allah created the pen, He said to it: "Write." It wrote what will exist until the Day of Resurrection. Allah, Exalted is He, says: (No calamity befalls on earth or in yourselves except that it is in a Book before We bring it into being). It has been said that this verse connects with what came before it, namely that Allah, Glorified is He, made light for them what afflicts them in jihad of killing and wounding, and explained that what keeps them from jihad, namely guarding wealth and what loss may befall it, is all written and decreed with no escape from it; the only duty upon a person is to obey the command. Then He taught them, saying this: (So that you do not despair over what has escaped you), i.e. so that you do not grieve over the provision that has passed you by. For when they know that provision has already been apportioned, they do not despair over what has escaped them of it. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that the Prophet ﷺ said: "None of you will find the sweetness of faith until he knows that what has befallen him would not have missed him, and what has missed him would not have befallen him." Then he recited: (So that you do not despair over what has escaped you), i.e. so that you do not grieve over what has escaped you of the worldly life, for it was not decreed for you; and had it been decreed for you, it would not have escaped you. The grief and exultation that are forbidden are those in which one transgresses into what is not permitted. Allah, Exalted is He, says: (Allah does not love every arrogant boaster) i.e. one who is proud of what he was given of worldly goods, boasting over people with it.

The recitation of the common readers is (atakum) with a long alif, i.e. He gave you of the worldly life. Abu Hatim preferred this. Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq said: O son of Adam, why do you grieve over what is lost, which the passing of time cannot return to you, or rejoice in what exists, which death will not leave in your hands? It was said to Barz Jumhur: "O wise one! Why do you not grieve over what has passed, nor rejoice in what is coming?" He said: "Because what has passed cannot be compensated by tears, and what is coming cannot be sustained by delight." Al-Fudayl ibn Iyad said on this meaning: The world is one that destroys and one that benefits; what it destroys has no return, and what it benefits announces departure. It was said: the arrogant (mukhtal) is one who looks at himself with the eye of pride, and the boastful (fakhur) is one who looks at people with the eye of contempt, and both are hidden shirk. The boastful is like a goat's udder that is tied so that milk gathers in it; the buyer imagines that this is its normal state, and it is not so. Likewise, one who sees in himself a state and adornment, while being a pretender, is the boastful.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who are stingy⦆ i.e. Allah does not love the arrogant (those who are stingy). (Those who are stingy) is in the place of a genitive as a description of (the arrogant). It was also said: it is nominative, as the subject, i.e. "those who are stingy, then Allah is free of them." It was said: he meant the Jewish leaders who withheld the description of Muhammad ﷺ that is in their books, lest people believe in him and their food be lost [[He means what they eat from people in the name of religion, in the form of wealth.]], as said by al-Suddi and al-Kalbi. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: (those who are stingy) means with knowledge, (and enjoin people to stinginess), i.e. not to teach people anything. Zayd ibn Aslam: it is stinginess in fulfilling the right of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It was also said: it is stinginess in giving charity and rights, as said by Amir ibn Abd Allah al-Ash'ari. Tawus said: it is stinginess with what is in one's hands. These three sayings are close in meaning. The people of insights (ashab al-khawatir) distinguished between stinginess and generosity in two ways: first, the stingy person delights in withholding, while the generous person delights in giving; second, the stingy person gives only when asked, while the generous person gives without being asked.

(And whoever turns away) i.e. from faith (then indeed Allah) is free of him. It is possible that, since He urged charity, He informed them that those who withhold it and enjoin people to withhold it, indeed Allah is free of them. The common reading is (bil-bukhl) with a damma on the ba' and a sukun on the kha'. Anas, Ubayd ibn Umayr, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, Mujahid, Humayd, Ibn Muhaysin, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (bil-bakhal) with two fathas, and this is the dialect of the Ansar. Abu al-Aliyah and Ibn al-Sumaiqa read (bil-bakhl) with a fatha on the ba' and sukun on the kha'. From Nasr ibn Asim (bil-bukul) with two dammas. All of these are well-known dialects. The distinction between bukhl and shuhh was already mentioned at the end of (Al 'Imran).

Nafi' and Ibn Amir read (fa-inna Allaha al-Ghaniyyu al-Hamid) without (huwa). The rest read (huwa al-Ghaniyyu) as a separator (fasl). It is also possible that it is a subject (mubtada'), with (al-Ghaniyyu) its predicate, and the whole clause is the predicate of inna. Whoever omits it, the better view is that it is a separator, because omitting a separator is easier than omitting a subject.

It was said: the arrogant (mukhtal) is one who looks at himself with the eye of pride, and the boastful (fakhur) is one who looks at people with the eye of contempt, and both are hidden shirk. The boastful is like a goat's udder that is tied so that milk gathers in it; the buyer imagines that this is its normal state, and it is not so. Likewise, one who sees in himself a state and adornment, while being a pretender, is the boastful.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who are stingy⦆ i.e. Allah does not love the arrogant (those who are stingy). (Those who are stingy) is in the place of a genitive as a description of (the arrogant). It was also said: it is nominative, as the subject, i.e. "those who are stingy, then Allah is free of them." It was said: he meant the Jewish leaders who withheld the description of Muhammad ﷺ that is in their books, lest people believe in him and their food be lost [[He means what they eat from people in the name of religion, in the form of wealth.]], as said by al-Suddi and al-Kalbi. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: (those who are stingy) means with knowledge, (and enjoin people to stinginess), i.e. not to teach people anything. Zayd ibn Aslam: it is stinginess in fulfilling the right of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It was also said: it is stinginess in giving charity and rights, as said by Amir ibn Abd Allah al-Ash'ari. Tawus said: it is stinginess with what is in one's hands. These three sayings are close in meaning. The people of insights (ashab al-khawatir) distinguished between stinginess and generosity in two ways: first, the stingy person delights in withholding, while the generous person delights in giving; second, the stingy person gives only when asked, while the generous person gives without being asked.

(And whoever turns away) i.e. from faith (then indeed Allah) is free of him. It is possible that, since He urged charity, He informed them that those who withhold it and enjoin people to withhold it, indeed Allah is free of them. The common reading is (bil-bukhl) with a damma on the ba' and a sukun on the kha'. Anas, Ubayd ibn Umayr, Yahya ibn Ya'mur, Mujahid, Humayd, Ibn Muhaysin, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (bil-bakhal) with two fathas, and this is the dialect of the Ansar. Abu al-Aliyah and Ibn al-Sumaiqa read (bil-bakhl) with a fatha on the ba' and sukun on the kha'. From Nasr ibn Asim (bil-bukul) with two dammas. All of these are well-known dialects. The distinction between bukhl and shuhh was already mentioned at the end of (Al 'Imran).

Nafi' and Ibn Amir read (fa-inna Allaha al-Ghaniyyu al-Hamid) without (huwa). The rest read (huwa al-Ghaniyyu) as a separator (fasl). It is also possible that it is a subject (mubtada'), with (al-Ghaniyyu) its predicate, and the whole clause is the predicate of inna. Whoever omits it, the better view is that it is a separator, because omitting a separator is easier than omitting a subject.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 57, verse 25–26:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs﴾, i.e., with clear miracles and manifest laws. It was also said: sincerity toward Allah, may He be exalted, in worship, and the establishment of prayer and the giving of zakah; with this the messengers called, from Noah and those after him down to Muhammad (ﷺ).

(And We sent down with them the Book) i.e., the books; that is, We revealed to them the report of what came before them. (And the Balance) Ibn Zayd said: it is that by which things are weighed and trade is conducted. (That people may maintain justice) i.e., justice in their dealings. His saying "with justice" indicates that He meant the familiar balance. Some people said: He meant by it justice. Al-Qushayri said: If we take it to mean the familiar balance, then the meaning is "We sent down the Book and set up the Balance," and it is of the type of the poet's words:

"I fed her chaff and cold water"

And this is supported by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the heaven He raised, and He set up the Balance﴾. Then He said: (And establish the weight with justice), and the discussion of this has already passed [[See p. 154 of this part.]].

(And We sent down iron, wherein is mighty violence) Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah sent down four blessings from the heaven to the earth: iron, fire, water and salt." Ikrimah related from Ibn Abbas, who said: Three things descended with Adam, peace be upon him: the Black Stone, which was whiter than snow; the staff of Musa, which was of the myrtle of Paradise, its length ten cubits along with Musa's height; and iron, with which three things descended: the anvil, the tongs, and the mi'qa'ah, which is the hammer. Al-Mawardi mentioned it. Al-Tha'labi said: Ibn Abbas said: Adam descended from Paradise and with him were five iron tools of the smiths: the anvil, the tongs, the mi'qa'ah, the hammer, and the needle. Al-Qushayri related it and said: The mi'qa'ah is that on which something is sharpened; it is said "waqa'tu al-hadidah aqa'uha," meaning I sharpened the iron. In al-Sihah: the mi'qa'ah is the place that the falcon frequents and alights upon, and the fuller's log on which cloth is beaten, and the hammer and the long whetstone. And it is narrated that iron was sent down on Tuesday.

(Wherein is mighty violence) i.e., for the shedding of blood. For this reason, bloodletting and cupping were forbidden on Tuesday, because it is a day on which blood flows. It is narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "On Tuesday there is an hour in which blood does not stop." It was also said: (We sent down iron) means We brought it into being and created it, like His saying, may He be exalted: (And He sent down for you of the cattle eight pairs) [[See vol. 15, p. 235]]. This is the saying of al-Hasan. Thus the iron would be from the earth, not sent down from the heaven. The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: i.e., He brought forth the iron from the ores and taught them its craft by His revelation.

(Wherein is mighty violence) meaning weapons, armour and shields. It was also said: i.e., in it is great fear of being killed.

(And benefits for people) Mujahid said: meaning protection (junnah). It was also said: meaning the benefit people derive from iron utensils, such as the knife, the axe, the needle and the like. (And that Allah may know who helps Him) i.e., We sent down iron so that Allah may know who helps Him. It was also said: this is coordinated with His saying, may He be exalted: (That people may maintain justice), i.e., We sent Our messengers and sent down the Book with them, and these things, so that people may deal with one another in truth, (and that Allah may know who helps Him) and that Allah may see who supports His religion (and) supports (His messengers in the unseen). Ibn Abbas said: they support them and do not deny them, and they believe in them (in the unseen), i.e., while they do not see them.

(Indeed Allah is Strong, Mighty) (Strong) in His seizing, (Mighty) i.e., invincible, dominant. This has already been mentioned. It was also said: (in the unseen) means with sincerity.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We certainly sent Noah and Abraham﴾. He elaborated what had been stated in summary concerning the sending of messengers with the Books, and informed that He sent Noah and Abraham and placed prophethood in their offspring: (And We placed in their descendants prophethood and the Book), i.e., We made some of their descendants prophets and some of them communities reciting the Books sent down from heaven: the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and the Furqan. Ibn Abbas said: the Book is writing by the pen. (Among them) i.e., among those who followed Abraham and Noah, (is one who is guided). It was also said: (Among them is one who is guided) means among their descendants are those who are guided.

(And many of them are defiant) disbelievers, going out of obedience.

He elaborated what had been stated in summary concerning the sending of messengers with the Books, and informed that He sent Noah and Abraham and placed prophethood in their offspring: (And We placed in their descendants prophethood and the Book), i.e., We made some of their descendants prophets and some of them communities reciting the Books sent down from heaven: the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms and the Furqan.
